questions.explanation: A turning point causes a lasting change of direction. Magna Carta established that even the king was under the law, an idea that outlasted the medieval period. The sakoku edicts cut Japan off from most foreign contact for over two centuries, shaping its whole development until 1853.
questions.question: In one sentence, explain why historians call the sealing of Magna Carta in 1215 OR the sakoku edicts of the 1630s a turning point.

questions.explanation: Model answer. Nobody knew about germs or that fleas on rats carried the disease. The Church taught that God sent suffering to punish sin, and when prayers did not stop the dying, many concluded that the sin must be very great, which is why some turned to extreme penance.
questions.question: Explain why many people in 1348 believed the plague was a punishment from God.

questions.explanation: Model answer. Samurai in debt to merchants, peasant uprisings and famines, or daimyo in the south-west (Satsuma, Choshu) resenting Tokugawa control.
questions.question: Give one piece of evidence that the Tokugawa shogunate was already weakening BEFORE Perry arrived.

questions.explanation: Land flowed down from the monarch to nobles to knights. Peasants worked the land at the bottom.
questions.question: Put the feudal hierarchy in order from the top. Which option is correct?
options: Monarch, knights, nobles, peasants
Monarch, nobles, knights, peasants
Nobles, monarch, knights, peasants
Monarch, nobles, peasants, knights

questions.explanation: The king could not be everywhere. Granting land made nobles responsible for defence and order in return for their oath.
questions.question: How did feudalism help a king control a large kingdom without a police force or a paid army?
options: Every peasant swore an oath of loyalty to the king in person and promised to fight for him when called
Nobles who held land from the king had to supply knights and keep order in their own regions
The Church policed the kingdom through its own courts and sent bishops to settle quarrels between nobles
The king kept all the land himself and sent royal sheriffs to collect rents and taxes from every village

questions.explanation: Trial by ordeal asked God to reveal guilt through the outcome. It was replaced by juries after 1215.
questions.question: A person accused of a crime carries a red-hot iron and the wound is checked three days later. This is...
options: trial by jury
trial by combat
trial by ordeal
a tithe

questions.explanation: Treason attacked the king himself and was punished by death and loss of all property.
questions.question: Which crime was punished most severely in medieval Europe?
options: Selling underweight bread
Poaching a rabbit
Treason against the king
Missing church

questions.explanation: A castle told everyone who ruled the region. The lord's court, treasury and soldiers were inside it.
questions.question: Besides defence, why were castles important to a lord's power?
options: They held the region's grain stores, so a lord could feed every village in his lands during a famine
They were a visible symbol of authority and the centre for collecting taxes and giving justice
They housed the peasants of the manor, who lived inside the walls and farmed the fields outside them
They were the centre of religious life, where the lord's own priest held mass for the whole village

questions.explanation: Stone resisted fire and siege engines. The purpose stayed the same while the form changed, which is continuity and change.
questions.question: How did castle design change between 1066 and 1300?
options: Stone keeps were replaced by cheaper wooden motte-and-bailey castles that could be built in a few weeks
Wooden motte-and-bailey castles were replaced by stone keeps and then concentric stone castles
Castle building stopped soon after 1100, because kings preferred to live in towns protected by stone walls
Stone walls were made thinner and lower, because gunpowder cannon could now knock down any high wall

questions.explanation: Monasteries were centres of learning, charity and medicine. They had nothing to do with training knights or collecting the king's taxes.
questions.question: Select ALL the ways a medieval monastery served the people around it.
options: Monks copied books by hand, preserving learning that would otherwise have been lost
Monasteries cared for the sick and gave food and shelter to travellers and the poor
Monasteries trained the lord's knights in warfare
Monasteries collected the king's taxes from the villages
Monks taught some boys to read, write and count

questions.explanation: Spiritual power came first. Land, wealth and political influence were built on it.
questions.question: What was the most important source of the Church's power in medieval Europe?
options: It commanded the largest army in Europe, made up of knights from the crusading orders
It controlled the path to heaven in a society where almost everyone feared hell
It owned about one third of Europe's farmland and collected a tithe from every villager
Its archbishops crowned kings, and its bishops sat as advisers on every royal council

questions.explanation: 1250 is in the 1200s, which is the 13th century. The Black Death came a century later.
questions.question: A source is captioned 'Illuminated manuscript, Paris, c. 1250'. Which statement about its origin is correct?
options: It was made in the 12th century
It was made in the 13th century
It was made in the 14th century
It was made after the Black Death

questions.explanation: Model answer. The Kamakura shogunate won a defensive war but had no conquered land to reward its samurai with, which weakened their loyalty and helped bring the shogunate down in 1333, while the storms that wrecked the Mongol fleets fed a lasting belief that Japan was protected by the gods.
questions.question: In one sentence, explain why the failed Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281 were a turning point for Japan.

questions.explanation: Model answer. The Crusades showed the Pope could unite kings and knights behind one cause and brought the Church land and wealth. The Black Death showed the Church could not stop or explain the plague, and many clergy died or fled.
questions.question: Give one way the Crusades strengthened the Catholic Church and one way the Black Death weakened it.
Edo grew from a small castle town in 1600 to a city of about a million people by 1700. Which Tokugawa policy did most to cause this growth?
options: Sankin kotai, which forced daimyo and their households to live in Edo every second year
Sakoku, which closed Japan's other ports so that all foreign trade had to pass through Nagasaki
The four-class system, which required all merchants and artisans to live in the shogun's capital
The ban on Christianity, which drove thousands of converts out of Kyushu to seek safety in Edo
questions.explanation: Alternate attendance filled Edo with daimyo households, their samurai and the merchants and craftspeople who served them. The constant demand for goods and services made Edo one of the largest cities in the world.

questions.question: Kabuki theatre, ukiyo-e woodblock prints and popular novels all flourished in Edo in the 1700s. Who was the main audience for this new culture?
options: Townspeople (chonin), especially merchants with money to spend
The emperor and his court nobles in the old capital of Kyoto
Farmers in the villages, who made up most of Japan's people
Buddhist monks and priests in the great temples of Edo and Kyoto
questions.explanation: Merchants ranked lowest officially but grew wealthy under two centuries of peace. Their money paid for a lively urban culture of theatres, prints, teahouses and fiction aimed at ordinary townspeople.

questions.question: Select ALL the ways the long Tokugawa peace changed the lives of samurai.
options: They increasingly worked as officials and administrators rather than fighting
Their fixed rice stipends bought less as prices rose, so many fell into debt
Many took up scholarship, poetry, tea ceremony and the arts
The samurai class was abolished by the shogun in 1700
Most samurai converted to Christianity
questions.explanation: Two centuries without war turned warriors into bureaucrats and scholars, while fixed stipends and rising prices left many samurai poorer than the merchants they outranked. The class survived until the Meiji reforms of the 1870s, and Christianity was banned.

questions.question: Travellers on the Tokaido had to stop at checkpoints such as Hakone, where officials searched for weapons being carried towards Edo and for women leaving it. What was the shogunate trying to prevent?
options: Daimyo smuggling guns into Edo, or their hostage families slipping out, which sankin kotai depended on
Merchants moving rice between domains without paying the shogun's tax on goods carried by road
Christian missionaries travelling in disguise from Nagasaki to preach in the shogun's capital
Peasants leaving their villages to look for paid work in the towns along the highway
questions.explanation: The checkpoints enforced sankin kotai. Guns entering Edo could arm a rebellion, and a daimyo's wife leaving Edo meant the hostage system was being evaded. The saying was 'incoming guns, outgoing women'.

questions.question: Post towns with inns, porters and horses grew up along the Tokaido and other highways during the Edo period. What created the demand for them?
options: Daimyo processions under sankin kotai, plus pilgrims, merchants and officials travelling the roads
Portuguese and Spanish merchants travelling to Edo to trade before sakoku expelled them in the 1630s
Samurai armies marching to and from the battles of the Sengoku period, which ended in 1600
Christian missionaries travelling between the churches they had built in Kyoto, Osaka and Edo
questions.explanation: Alternate attendance sent thousands of people up and down the highways every year, and the roads became busy with pilgrims and traders as well.

questions.question: Put these periods of Japanese history in the correct order, earliest first.
options: Heian, Kamakura, Muromachi, Edo
Kamakura, Heian, Edo, Muromachi
Muromachi, Kamakura, Heian, Edo
Heian, Muromachi, Kamakura, Edo
questions.explanation: Heian (794 to 1185) was the age of the imperial court. Kamakura (1185 to 1333) began with the first shogun. Muromachi (1336 to 1573) was the age of the Ashikaga shoguns. Edo (1603 to 1868) was the Tokugawa period, named for the shogun's capital.

questions.question: A timeline shows the Onin War in 1467 and Tokugawa Ieyasu becoming shogun in 1603. Which century does each belong to?
options: 15th century and 17th century
14th century and 16th century
15th century and 16th century
16th century and 17th century
questions.explanation: To find the century, add one to the hundreds digit. 1467 is in the 1400s, so the 15th century. 1603 is in the 1600s, so the 17th century. Be careful with round years: 1600 itself is the last year of the 16th century.

questions.question: Which of these happened during the Kamakura period (1185 to 1333)?
options: The Mongol invasions of Japan
Perry's arrival in Edo Bay
The Tokugawa sakoku edicts
The outbreak of the Onin War
questions.explanation: The Mongols attacked in 1274 and 1281, under the Kamakura shogunate. The Onin War was 1467 (Muromachi), sakoku the 1630s and Perry 1853 (both Edo).

questions.question: A history book shows a painted folding screen of Portuguese traders arriving at Nagasaki, made in Japan around 1600. How should this source be described?
options: A primary source: a visual (artwork) created at the time it depicts
A secondary source: a picture reproduced in a book published long after 1600
A primary source: a written document from the period about foreign trade
A secondary source: an artwork made by someone who was not a historian
questions.explanation: Type of source means the form it takes: a screen, print, letter, chronicle, map and so on. Origin means who made it, where and when. A screen painted around 1600 showing the traders of its own day is a primary visual source regardless of where it is reproduced today.

questions.question: A caption reads: 'Stained-glass window made in Canterbury, England, c. 1180, maker unknown.' Which of these can you state from the caption alone?
options: Where and roughly when it was made
The purpose the artist had in mind
Whether the scene really happened
The name of the person who paid for it
questions.explanation: Captions usually give origin: place, date and (if known) creator. Purpose, accuracy and patron have to be inferred from the content and your own knowledge, and you should signal that with words like 'suggests' or 'implies'.

questions.question: A medieval illumination shows a king on his throne while a noble kneels and places his hands between the king's. Write one sentence that INFERS something about power from the picture, using the word 'suggests'.
questions.explanation: A good inference links a detail to a conclusion: 'The noble kneeling with his hands in the king's suggests that loyalty was a personal promise made in public, which bound the vassal to his lord.' Weak answers only describe what is in the picture.

terms.definition: An area that contains a chain or group of islands scattered in lakes, rivers or the ocean.
The code of behaviour of the samurai that required honour, loyalty (even to death), good living, thrift and martial arts skill.
The link between what causes an action or motivates someone to act in a certain way, and the outcome of that action.
The religion based on the person and teachings of Jesus Christ.
People ordained for religious duties, especially in the Christian church.
The recognition that while many things change over time, some quite drastically, other things continue, even if in modified forms.
A series of wars fought by Christians and Muslims between 1096 and 1291 CE over control of the Holy Land.
A Japanese lord, vassal to the shogun.
An official order issued by the shogun or another authority in Japan that people were expected to obey.
A sovereign ruler of great power and rank. Under the shogunate the emperor was a ceremonial and religious figurehead while governing power was in the hands of the shogun.
The information or clues discovered by asking specific questions about a historical source.
A religious punishment that cut someone off from the church community and its sacraments, such as communion, confession and entry to heaven.
A set of legal and military customs that organised the society of medieval Europe. A lord gave a fief to a vassal in exchange for loyalty and support.
Land given by a lord to a vassal in medieval Europe in return for loyalty and service.
A group of radical Christians during the Black Death who whipped themselves to gain God's forgiveness for their sins.
Doing or saying something regarded by the medieval Catholic Church as being in serious conflict with its teachings.
A way of organising people so that the most important is at the top, with others ranked underneath in decreasing order of importance. Social hierarchy arranges people according to power and wealth.
A medieval warrior of Europe who pledged his services to a lord, sometimes to a king, in exchange for a fief.
A king or queen who administered the country, planned or fought wars and owned the land on which they ruled. The monarch sat at the top of the social hierarchy.
Wealthy subjects who lived on land granted to them (fiefs) in large manor houses. They were below the monarch on the social hierarchy.
The largest group in medieval society, who undertook the bulk of physical work, most of it related to farming.
The way a person or particular people view some aspect of the past. Perspectives are shaped by prejudices, fears, uncertainties, age, gender and education.

Japan's policy of national seclusion under the Tokugawa (1630s to 1853). Japanese people could not leave and most foreigners could not enter, on pain of death. Limited trade with the Dutch and Chinese continued at Nagasaki.
A Japanese medieval warrior who lived by the bushido code and was loyal to his daimyo.
A Tokugawa system that required daimyo to reside in Edo for periods of time, alternating with residence at their own castle.
A medieval peasant who worked on the manor of a feudal lord and was bound to that land.
The title given to Japan's top military rulers between the 12th and 19th centuries.
The importance of an event, person or development in the past, judged by how much it changed people's lives or how it helps us understand history today.
One tenth of annual produce or earnings, taken as a contribution for the support of the Catholic Church and clergy.
The crime of betraying the king, for example plotting against him or helping his enemies. It was punished more severely than any other crime.
An event or development that leads to a major change in the direction of history.
Under feudalism, a person who offered loyalty and service to a lord in return for protection and the granting of a fief.
A process whereby societies adopt what is considered to be Western culture in areas such as industry, technology, science, education, politics, law and social norms.
794 to 1185. The age of the imperial court, when the emperor and noble families such as the Fujiwara held power and the samurai class first emerged.
1185 to 1333. Began when Minamoto Yoritomo became the first shogun after the Genpei War. Japan came under military rule and repelled the Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281.
1603 to 1868. The rule of the Tokugawa shoguns from Edo (Tokyo). A time of peace, sakoku, strict social order and the growth of cities and merchant culture.
The code of conduct expected of a knight: courage in battle, loyalty to his lord, protection of the Church and the weak, and courtesy, especially towards noblewomen.
A lord's estate in medieval Europe: his house or castle, the village, the farmland worked by peasants and the common land. The manor was the basic unit of feudal life.

A medieval way of deciding guilt by a painful test, such as carrying a hot iron or being lowered into cold water, in the belief that God would protect the innocent. Replaced by trial by jury after the Church banned priests from taking part in 1215.
The plague that reached Europe in 1347 and killed between a third and a half of the population within five years, spread along trade routes by fleas on rats and from person to person.
The 1854 agreement that Commodore Perry forced on the shogunate, opening two ports to American ships and ending more than 200 years of sakoku.
The return of power from the shogun to the emperor in 1868, after which Japan modernised rapidly: a new government, a conscript army, industry, railways and Western-style education.
Compulsory military service. Introduced in Japan in 1873, so that ordinary men of all classes were drafted into a modern army, ending the samurai's role as the only warriors.
Popular Japanese theatre with music, dance and dramatic costume that flourished in Edo and Osaka during the Tokugawa period, performed for ordinary townspeople rather than the samurai elite.
'Pictures of the floating world': colour woodblock prints of actors, landscapes and city life, made cheaply for townspeople in the Edo period. Hokusai and Hiroshige were ukiyo-e artists.
